posts.title: Yuzu on the longest night
posts.excerpt: On the winter solstice the deep tub fills with floating yuzu, and the whole street smells of it.
posts.content:
On the winter solstice we float a crate of yuzu in the deep tub. The fruit bob against your shoulders and the steam smells of citrus for the whole evening.

The custom is said to keep colds away until spring. Whether or not it works, it is the busiest night of the year; come early, and leave the fruit in the water.

posts.title: Iris leaves in May
posts.excerpt: Bundles of iris leaves in the shallow tub for Children's Day, and why the children stay in longer than usual.
posts.content:
On the fifth of May bundles of iris leaves go into the shallow tub. They are sharp and green and smell faintly of cut grass.

Children are told the leaves make them strong. They stay in the water twice as long as on any other day, which is the real purpose.

posts.title: The mural repaint
posts.excerpt: One closed Monday every six years, Noriko Seta repaints the mountain above the tubs in a single day.
posts.content:
The tubs are drained on Sunday night. By seven on Monday morning Noriko Seta is on a plank across the deep tub with four tins of blue and a broom-sized brush.

She finishes before dusk, every time. One small thing is always different afterwards; this year nobody has found it yet.

posts.title: A night with the boiler
posts.excerpt: From one in the afternoon until midnight, Kenta keeps the fire going with offcuts from the joinery.
posts.content:
The boiler is older than Kenta and louder than the street. He lights it at one, feeds it timber offcuts every forty minutes, and listens to it more than he looks at it.

At midnight the fire is let down, the tubs are drained and scrubbed, and the chimney goes quiet until the next afternoon.

posts.title: Why the milk is so cold
posts.excerpt: The glass case in the changing room, the small dairy that fills it, and the right way to drink it.
posts.content:
The milk comes twice a week from a small dairy in the hills, in the same short glass bottles it has always come in. The case is set colder than any fridge at home.

You drink it standing, after the bath, before your hair is dry. Plain is the classic; the coffee milk sells out first.

posts.title: Your first time at a sento
posts.excerpt: A short walk through a first visit, from the curtain to the bench, for anyone who has never been.
posts.content:
Pay at the front desk, take a towel if you need one, and go through the curtain for your side. Undress in the changing room and leave everything in a basket or a locker.

Wash at a tap first, then soak. Nobody minds that you are new; the regulars were all new once, usually as small children holding a grandparent's hand.
